operations.name: Peter Bianki

expected.name: Peter Bianki
expected.description:
Peter Bianki was born 1891 in Odessa, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a laborer, metal worker, printer. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Born to Italian immigrant parents to Russia. Hoined the Union of Russian Workers shortly after its founding in 1914. Quickly became one of its prominent leaders. Elected URW Secretary in January 1919 and later editor of its newspaper Khleb i Volia. Married to Nadia Bianki. Arrested in New York in February 1919 and deported on the Buford on December 21, 1919. 

In Russia, quickly joined the Communist Party and held multiple Soviet government posts. During the Kronstadt mutiny, however, he shot himself in the arm to avoid being conscripted into military action against it. In 1928 transferred to Siberia to direct a grain-requisitioning detachment; killed in March 1930 during an armed peasant uprising, and was afterward celebrated as a Communist martyr.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

operations.research_note: Zimmer explicitly says killed March1930; no named criminal charge.

operations.name: Malachi O'Neill

expected.name: Malachi O'Neill
expected.description: Malachi O'Neill was one of the 74 Industrial Workers of the World members held in the Snohomish County jail and charged with murder after the Everett Massacre. On November 5, 1916, some 300 Industrial Workers of the World members sailed from Seattle to Everett, Washington aboard the steamers Verona and Calista to support a shingle-weavers' strike and the IWW's free-speech fight. At the Everett dock, Snohomish County sheriff Donald McRae and a posse of armed vigilantes opened fire on the Verona, killing at least five Wobblies and wounding dozens. The returning IWW members were arrested, and 74 were charged with the murder of two deputies (Jefferson Beard and Charles Curtis) killed in the gunfire. Only Thomas H. Tracy was brought to trial; after his acquittal on May 5, 1917, the charges against the others were dropped. At the time of the massacre he was 34, a blacksmith, born in Ireland.

operations.research_note: Yale booking photograph catalog names Malachai O'Neill. Birth circa 1877 conflicts with existing 1882; preserve pending original booking verification. No sentence warranted after dismissal; no exact May release day established.

operations.name: Melinda Jones-Williams

expected.name: Melinda Jones-Williams
expected.description:
Melinda Jones-Williams was one of the Black school-aged girls imprisoned in southwest Georgia in 1963 after participating in demonstrations against racial segregation in Americus. Authorities moved girls arrested during the campaign to the Lee County Stockade in neighboring Leesburg, concealed their location from their families, and held them without formal criminal charges. Survivor and commemorative accounts identify her with the long-held group and describe approximately two months of confinement; the exact endpoints vary among accounts. The children endured overcrowding, inadequate food and water, broken sanitation, little or no bedding, and delayed medical attention. SNCC photographer Danny Lyon documented the confinement through the bars; publication of his photographs helped force public attention and the girls’ release.

She appears in the identified Danny Lyon group photograph and later worked as a computer operator for New Jersey Bell Telephone Company.

Photo: Danny Lyon, August 1963; via The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. Original-image crop; identified by the source (first named standing subject from left in caption). Source: https://www.ajc.com/news/state--regional/girls-imprisoned-leesburg-stockade-get-state-historical-marker/uGgSuxRrOxw6LANKGmuHpK/ . Copyright status unconfirmed; used for educational biographical identification at the site owner's direction. No permission or open license claimed.
expected.body:
## The Leesburg Stockade

In the summer of 1963, young people in Americus, Georgia demonstrated against segregation, including the Martin Theater’s separate entrances and ticket windows. Local authorities arrested hundreds of participants. More than 30 Black girls were held at different times in the Lee County Stockade in nearby Leesburg without formal charges or a court hearing.

Contemporary sworn statements show that the girls did not all enter or leave together. They describe changing populations of roughly 32 to 35 children, overflowing or unusable toilets, contaminated bedding, undercooked food, rusty water, and periods when the children slept directly on concrete. The profile’s custody dates and duration are therefore individual where evidence permits; no universal 45-day range has been imposed.

SNCC photographer Danny Lyon photographed the girls and the stockade conditions. The resulting photographs circulated through movement publications and the Black press and helped expose where the children were being held.

operations.research_note: Congressional Record March 11, 2019 recognition explicitly gives birth March 14, 1950. Leesburg confinement without formal charges does not justify inventing charges or exact individual September release.

operations.name: Roberto Elia

expected.name: Roberto Elia
expected.description: Roberto Elia was an Italian anarchist printer born in Catanzaro on July 29, 1871. Active as a socialist in Italy from 1898, he was repeatedly arrested for political activity. After immigrating to the United States, he worked for Carlo Tresca’s La Plebe in Pittsburgh and Luigi Galleani’s Cronaca Sovversiva in Barre, Vermont, before relocating to Boston and New York. He belonged to the Gruppo Gaetano Bresci in East Harlem and published the anarchist journals Domani and L’Ordine. Federal agents took Elia and fellow printer Andrea Salsedo into custody without warrants on February 25, 1920, suspecting them of printing leaflets connected with the 1919 anarchist bombings. They were held incommunicado in the Bureau of Investigation’s Manhattan offices. Salsedo died in a fall from the building in May. Elia was later transferred to Ellis Island and deported to Italy on August 7, 1920. He remained active in the Italian anarchist movement and died of tuberculosis in 1924.

operations.research_note: Italian historical institute biographical dictionary explicitly gives Naples June 11, 1924 death, refining existing year.

expected.name: Alexander Bukovetsky
expected.description:
Alexander Bukovetsky was born 1886 in Born , Ekaterinoslav, Russia (present-day Dnipro, Ukraine). Worked as a metalworker.

Joined the Socialist-Revolutionary Party as a youth and participated in the 1905 Russian Revolution. Migrated with his wife Frances and their daughter to Canada, where a son was born. Became an anarchist in Ontario; moved between the United States and Canada repeatedly for work. Arrested in March 1918 after giving radical speech in Timmins, Ontario, but the charges were dropped. Migrated to the US with family the following year, and employed as a machinist at the Ford Motor Company. Active in the Union of Russian Workers in Detroit and organized URW branches in Jackson and Kalamazoo, Michigan. Arrested in Detroit in January 1920 and detained at Fort Wayne, where on one occasion guards beat him bloody in front of his visiting wife and children. During his detainment, Frances was diagnosed with tuberculosis and the family was “dependent upon the charity of friends for support.” At their request, the entire family was deported February 26, 1921 (Frances being deported as an immigrant who entered the US illegally and was “likely to become a public charge”). 

After arrival in Soviet Russia he immediately spoke out against the Communist dictatorship and was arrested as a Makhnovist supporter. Frances obtained his release with the assistance of anarchists including Emma Goldman, and the family emigrated to Germany and then Windsor, Canada, where they remained active in the Russian-speaking anarchist movement. Frances died in 1935; Alexander (under the name “Felix Konosevich”) died in 1954.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.
expected.body:
Photograph: Alexander Bukovetsky (also Bukhovetsky/Felix Konosevich), Windsor, circa 1940s; published in Delo Truda-Probuzhdenie, January-April 1954. Reproduced by Kenyon Zimmer. The source image is preserved unaltered.

Date review: The source distinguishes the dismissed 1918 Canadian case from the January 1920 Detroit arrest and Fort Wayne detention. Month precision is retained. February 26, 1921 remains the deportation endpoint.

expected.name: Severn Teackle Wallis
expected.description: Severn Teackle Wallis was a distinguished Baltimore lawyer and man of letters and a member of the Maryland House of Delegates. He was among the roughly thirty state legislators and officials seized in the September 1861 federal arrests meant to prevent a feared secession vote, and was imprisoned without charge at Fort McHenry and then Fort Warren for some fourteen months.
